title: Evaluating models and overfitting
summary: MAE, RMSE and R², baselines, and why the training score lies.

steps.title: How wrong is the model?
body: Three standard regression metrics, all from the errors `e = y - y_hat`:
mae  = np.mean(np.abs(e))                  # mean absolute error, in y's units
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(e ** 2))            # punishes big misses more
**R²** compares the model with the dumbest sensible model, "always predict the mean": 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the mean, and on a test set it can even go negative.
MAE is easy to explain ("off by 12k on average"); RMSE is larger when a few predictions are very wrong.

steps.explain: Errors are -2, 2, 0 and -10. MAE averages their sizes: 14 / 4 = 3.5. RMSE squares first, so the single miss of 10 dominates: sqrt(108 / 4) = 5.2.

steps.title: Regression metrics
steps.prompt: Write `mae(y, y_hat)`, `rmse(y, y_hat)` and `r2(y, y_hat)`, each returning a plain float rounded to 3 decimals. Inputs may be lists or arrays.
hints: Start each with `e = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) - np.asarray(y_hat, dtype=float)`.
template: Dojo.eq("predicting the mean gives r2 = 0", 0.0, r2(_y, [25, 25, 25, 25]))
Dojo.check("worse than the mean gives negative r2", r2(_y, [40, 30, 20, 10]) < 0, "")

steps.prompt: Your model scores R² = 0.0 on the test set. What does that tell you?
options: It predicts no better than always guessing the mean of the target
It predicts the opposite of the truth

steps.title: Always beat a baseline
body: A metric means little alone. "RMSE 41k" might be great or terrible. Compare against a **baseline**: the simplest prediction that needs no model, such as the **training mean** of the target for regression, or the most common class for classification.
If your model does not clearly beat the baseline on the test set, it has not learned anything useful yet.

steps.title: Model versus baseline
prompt: Write `compare_to_baseline(y_train, y_test, pred)` returning a dict:
- `"baseline_mae"`: MAE of always predicting the **training** mean;
- `"improvement"`: `1 - model_mae / baseline_mae` (from unrounded values), as a fraction.
hints: The baseline prediction for every test row is `np.mean(y_train)`.
`1 - model / base` with the unrounded MAEs.
template: Dojo.check("a useless model shows no improvement", compare_to_baseline([1, 3], [2, 2], [5, 5])["improvement"] < 0, "")

items: Training error tiny, test error large
Training and test error both large
A straight line through clearly curved data

steps.title: Overfitting, seen
body: More flexible models fit the training data better **always**, but past some point they start fitting the noise, and the test error rises again.

Pick the complexity with the lowest error on data the model did not train on, never on training error. (With only a test set, you will soon want a separate **validation** set or cross-validation, so the test set stays untouched until the end.)

steps.title: Find the sweet spot
prompt: Write `poly_errors(x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test, degrees)` returning `{degree: (train_rmse, test_rmse)}` (plain floats, rounded to 3) using `np.polyfit` / `np.polyval`, and `best_degree(errors)` returning the degree with the lowest **test** RMSE.
Then draw the two curves: `plt.plot(degrees, train, label="train")` and `plt.plot(degrees, test, label="test")`, with `plt.legend()`, x label `"degree"` and y label `"RMSE"`, inside `poly_errors`.
The tests use noisy data from a cubic curve.
solution: def poly_errors(x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test, degrees):
plt.plot(degrees, [errors[d][0] for d in degrees], label="train")
plt.plot(degrees, [errors[d][1] for d in degrees], label="test")
hints: `min(errors, key=lambda d: errors[d][1])` picks the lowest test error.
template: Dojo.check("training error never rises with degree", _e[1][0] >= _e[3][0] >= _e[9][0], str(_e))
Dojo.check("degree 9 overfits: its test error is worse than degree 3", _e[9][1] > _e[3][1], str(_e))
Dojo.eq("legend labels", ["train", "test"], [t.get_text() for t in _ax.get_legend().get_texts()] if _ax.get_legend() else [])
